text: Now let's see how a semantic model is actually built in Salesforce. Product names and features here are changing quickly, so treat the specifics as accurate as of this writing, and check current release notes before relying on any detail.

This is the real Semantic Model Builder. On the left, a Model panel lists metrics, parameters, logical views, and data objects. On the canvas, the objects and their relationships. Here the Opportunity object is selected, with its outline and a data preview. The builder is available in Tableau Next and in Data 360, formerly Data Cloud.

Calculated fields hold logic the raw data lacks. This is the real calculated field dialog, with a formula editor, field type, and data type. There is also a Draft with Einstein option that proposes a formula from a plain-language prompt. Treat any drafted formula as a starting point, and review it carefully.

Follow a simple workflow. Add the data objects that answer the business question. Define the relationships. Add calculated fields. Define metrics. Then test the model against numbers you already trust, like a native report. That last step is where your earlier Salesforce reporting skills pay off.

One model, many consumers. Tableau Next visualizations and dashboards. Metrics and their insights. Conversational, AI-assisted analytics. And Tableau Desktop or Tableau Cloud, through the Tableau Semantics connector. That reach is why the modeling investment is worth it.
Remember that CRM Analytics uses its own datasets and SAQL, while semantic models are a Data 360 and Tableau Next construct. Next up: avoiding metric drift.
